Houston Texans|Buffalo Bills.read: The 4.9-point gap comes almost entirely from the base power ratings: the model has Houston (3.65) rated 1.5 points better than Buffalo (2.13) plus home field, while the market prices Buffalo as the better team and a road favorite. The injury slate is negligible and symmetric — all Q15 listings, net roughly -0.10 for Houston (Anderson/McDonald) and -0.04 for Buffalo (Sanders/Johnson) — so there is no unpriced availability information here. This is a rating disagreement about team quality, not a lineup delta, and with early-season 2026 ratings the far more likely explanation is drift in the model's Bills/Texans ratings than the market being 5 points wrong on a marquee matchup. The 1-star (8.5%) tag confirms the model itself has low conviction, and Walters' rule is that disagreement is not edge. A 4.9-point number on a well-bet AFC game with no injury catalyst is a signal to re-check the ratings rather than a signal to bet. Pass, or at most a token lean Houston +1.5 if the rating gap survives a rating audit.
Houston Texans|Buffalo Bills.risks: If the model's Houston edge is real (offensive line protection units are near-identical and rush units slightly favor Buffalo, so no unit-level driver), passing forfeits a large-line value; conversely, betting Houston on a stale rating exposes you to a road-favorite market that is usually sharp. Any of the Q15 players (especially Anderson) being downgraded to out would move the true delta but only by a fraction of a point.

Los Angeles Chargers|Arizona Cardinals.read: The model lands at 6.99 versus a market of 9.5, and essentially all of that 2.5-point gap comes from the base power ratings (0.86 vs -4.09 plus 2 HFA), not from injuries: the listed questionable tags are backups or negligible deltas (Leonard -0.02, Adams -0.06, Taylor-Demerson ~0) and net to almost nothing on either side. That means this is not an information edge from unpriced availability; it is a rating-level disagreement, likely the market grading Arizona lower (or the Chargers higher) than our numbers after Week 1 results, or our ratings drifting slowly. The 1-star flag (~7%) marks it as a genuine but small disagreement, and 2.5 points crossing 7 through 9 is a meaningful chunk of key numbers, which nudges toward the dog. Because the disagreement is rating-based rather than injury-based, treat it as a modest lean on Arizona +9.5 rather than a conviction play; if the market steps to 10 the value improves, if it drops toward 8 the edge is mostly gone.
Los Angeles Chargers|Arizona Cardinals.risks: The gap may reflect legitimate market information about Arizona's early-season form that the ratings have not yet absorbed (rating drift against us, not for us); the unit metrics show the Cardinals with weak rush efficiency and mediocre protection, so a Chargers blowout covering a big number is plausible. The O/U gap of 1.9 points is below actionable threshold. Line movement toward 8 would eliminate the edge.

Las Vegas Raiders|Miami Dolphins.read: The disagreement is almost entirely rating-based: our power numbers have Las Vegas (-4.58) and Miami (-3.56) as near-equal bad teams, producing a base of roughly 1 point with HFA, while the market has the Raiders as a 3-point home favorite -- a gap of about 2.1 points. The only injury input is Bowers listed questionable with Mayer a near-equivalent replacement (-0.09), so there is no availability information here the market could plausibly be missing; this is a difference in team valuation, not information. Early-season (Week 2) power ratings are the noisiest they will be all year and this looks like drift or a differing read on two low-rated rosters rather than a mispriced number, and the unit-level rush/protection adjustments are already baked in and near zero. Two stars is disagreement, not edge; without an information catalyst and with the line sitting on the key number of 3, the Walters discipline is to pass rather than fade the market on rating opinion alone. If Bowers were downgraded to out and the market didn't move, that would tilt slightly toward Miami +3, but the backup delta is too small to matter.
Las Vegas Raiders|Miami Dolphins.risks: Early-season ratings could be systematically off on either team, so both the side and the 2.2-point total edge (model 42.4 vs 40.2) fall inside normal rating error; Bowers' status could change and the 3 is a key number that makes price movement expensive to chase.

Indianapolis Colts|Baltimore Ravens.read: The 5.2-point gap is entirely a power-rating disagreement: both rosters are full strength, so there is no injury delta the market could have missed and no information edge to point to. Our ratings have Baltimore (1.67) and Indianapolis (1.37) as near-equivalent average teams, so HFA makes the Colts a 1.7-point favorite, while the market has the Ravens laying 3.5 on the road, implying it rates Baltimore roughly 5 points better than we do. That kind of gap on a Week 2 game with clean injury reports is the signature of rating drift or stale priors on our side, not a mispriced market; the market has a Lamar Jackson-led Ravens team in the top tier and our number likely hasn't caught up. The unit adjustments (Colts protection -0.037, Ravens rush -0.039) are noise-level and already baked in, so they explain none of the difference. Stars measure disagreement, not edge, and one star at 8.5% with no informational catalyst is a pass; if forced, the lean is Colts +3.5 at the home number, but this is not a Walters-grade position.
Indianapolis Colts|Baltimore Ravens.risks: Our ratings may simply be wrong on Baltimore, so the home lean could be fading a correctly priced favorite; the 2.1-point total gap (49.9 vs 47.8) is a mild over lean but within normal totals noise. Watch for late-week injury news that would convert this from a rating disagreement into actual information.

Carolina Panthers|Chicago Bears.read: The model has Chicago as a narrow ~1-point favorite while the market has them -3, a 1.9-point gap worth 1.5 stars. None of that gap comes from availability: the listed injuries are all Q15 with backups nearly at par (Jones II -0.07, Jarrett -0.03, Thuney and Bagent essentially zero), so there is no injury information the market could be missing. The disagreement is therefore entirely a power-rating difference — the market values the Bears roughly two points higher than our ratings, which reads as rating drift or a market read on Chicago's offseason improvement rather than a mispricing we can source. Under the Walters framework a 1.5-star, information-free gap is a lean at best (toward Carolina +3), not a play; it sits below the threshold where our ratings have shown reliable edge. The 3 is also a key number, which makes Carolina +3 more attractive than +2.5 would be, but not enough to overcome the lack of a catalyst.
Carolina Panthers|Chicago Bears.risks: If Bears are being bet up on legitimate offseason information (QB development, line upgrades) our rating is simply stale and the lean is wrong; Bagent listed as Q for the away QB slot suggests a possible unsettled QB situation that could cut either way; total gap of 1.8 (45.5 vs 47.3) is too small to act on and may reflect the same rating drift.

Cincinnati Bengals|Tampa Bay Buccaneers.read: The base line from ratings plus HFA is about +1.0 for Cincinnati, and the only injury input is Jonathan Allen at Q15 with a tiny -0.06 delta versus Slaton, so the model sits at 0.95 while the market has the Bengals at -3.5. That 2.5-point gap is not injury information -- Tampa is full strength and the Allen situation is nearly a wash -- so the disagreement is almost entirely a rating dispute: the market is treating Cincinnati as roughly a 3-point better team than our power numbers do, likely pricing offensive personnel or early-season perception that the ratings have not moved on. With no availability edge and a 1-star (8.5%) disagreement, this is a weak market-drift lean rather than a Walters-grade information play, but 2.5 points on a low-total NFL spread with the model getting the road team as a short dog is enough for a small position. The unit numbers show both teams below average in rushing and protection, with Tampa's protection markedly worse, which cuts slightly against the away side but is already in the ratings.
Cincinnati Bengals|Tampa Bay Buccaneers.risks: Rating drift may be ours, not the market's -- if Cincinnati's offense is stronger than the power number implies, the market is right and the edge evaporates; Allen's Q15 status could flip to out with negligible impact; small sample early-season ratings are the least reliable of the year; O/U gap of 0.5 is inside noise.
